1.explanation: All of the logic for highlighting TS generics lives in src/languages/typescript.js, which builds on the generic modes defined in src/languages/lib/ecmascript.js. In typescript.js there is a “title” mode (via hljs.TITLE_MODE or similar) that matches generic-type identifiers but only consumes the first camel-case segment (letters until the transition to a lone capital). The underlying ecmascript.js also contributes shared generic syntax rules. To fix the issue, the identifier regex in these files must be adjusted so that OutT (or any mixed-case identifier ending in a capital) is recognized as one token rather than two.
1.bug_scenario: When you write a TypeScript generic type with a camel-cased type parameter—e.g. OutT—the highlighter only treats “Out” as a single title token and leaves the trailing “T” un-styled (or styled differently). In other words, the regex/mode that picks up type parameters in the TS grammar is splitting the camel-case identifier at the capital-letter boundary instead of consuming the entire word.

2.explanation:
1. src/languages/typescript.js: This file extends the JavaScript/ECMAScript grammar to add TypeScript‐specific parsing, including generic parameter lists (`<OutT, InT>`) and the rules for classifying those identifiers as type names. The broken behavior lives in the clause that detects and highlights angle-bracketed identifiers.  
2. src/languages/lib/ecmascript.js: The TypeScript mode inherits the base identifier and keyword regexes from the ECMAScript grammar. The way ECMA’s identifier rules (and keyword/title modes) are constructed here feeds into how TypeScript’s generics get split. A fix often requires adjusting the base definition so it doesn’t break on camel-case transitions.  
3. src/lib/utils.js: Some of the internal utility functions (e.g. those that split or normalize identifier text for lookups) inadvertently inject a camel-case boundary split. Those helpers participate in feeding tokens to the grammar engine, so they can be responsible for splitting “OutT” into “Out” + “T” before the highlighter ever applies type-identifier styling.
2.bug_scenario: When you write a TypeScript generic type with a multi-segment identifier like “OutT” or “InT” in a code block, highlight.js only applies your type-name styling to “Out” (or “In”) and then treats the trailing “T” as a separate un-styled token. In other words, the camel-cased generic parameter name gets split into two runs — the first chunk gets the proper “type” highlight, the second chunk does not.
